newsitem.title: UK: Jerusalem Israel's capital "for ever" - Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Jerusalem Israel's capital "for ever" - Netanyahu.

text.p: The status of Jerusalem is not up for negotiation and the city will be Israel's capital for ever, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in an interview published on Tuesday in Britain's Financial Times newspaper.
The previous Labour government postponed the building of the Har Homa settlement in Jerusalem, but Netanyahu appeared to have no qualms about supporting its construction, the newspaper said.

"What you are really saying is that it is provocative for Israel to build in its capital. It is like saying: Why don't you stop building in London or Dublin?', because somebody is saying it's not your capital," Netanyahu said.
Israel is expected to discuss the status of Jerusalem and Israel's future borders in talks with the Palestinian authorities due to start in a few weeks.
However, the Financial Times said Netanyahu was "quick to respond" to any suggestion that Jerusalem's final status had still to be settled.
"Jerusalem was, is and will be the Israeli capital for ever," he said, adding that the government was building for Arabs and Christians as well as the Jewish residents.

On the question of borders, Netanyahu said the Golan Heights had "strategic valuable territory for Israel", but, on the other hand, Israel was ready to leave southern Lebanon "yesterday, let alone tomorrow".
"But we will do so when we have arrangements on the ground," he said, with the Lebanese army filling the security vacuum that would be left behind.

"This is not happening because Syria is effectively vetoing the proposal," he said, adding: "It would be very difficult to envisage how we can sustain negotiations for peace while a proxy war is being conducted against Israel."

Asked if he expected to see a Palestinian state during his premiership, Netanyahu replied: "If you ask me point blank, I say I would oppose it for the simple reason that the word state' encompasses sovereign powers that could threaten our survival."
"But if you talk about self-government -- legal and local powers and (the authority to) raise taxes -- I think a balance could be struck between their needs and our need for protection."
Netanyahu said the recent strength of the Tel Aviv stock exchange showed that international investors accepted his government was committed to the peace process.

He said the sell-off of state-owned Bank Hapoalim -- Israel's biggest bank -- was a top priority, and would be "a milestone in the break-up of the concentration of the Israeli economy". It could go ready "in about three months".
"Bank Hapoalim controls eight percent of GDP," he said. "There is no such concentration of wealth or economic power in any other western economy."
